claims.text: Morgan Stanley, Merrill and Raymond James each take a distinct approach to advisor recruiting and retention: Morgan Stanley recruits selectively through its advisor-led channel atop its integrated platform, Merrill pairs an internal training program with experienced-advisor hiring, and Raymond James leads with culture and multiple affiliation options, preferring one-by-one recruiting.

Morgan Stanley recruits financial advisors through its advisor-led channel, while also receiving flows into that channel from its workplace funnel, and attributes recruiting interest to the platform it has invested in.

Merrill is picking up the recruiting of experienced advisors, but this is not an enormous part of its strategy; its core approach is a training program that trains people in wealth management at Bank of America and Merrill, which the firm believes drives net new flows.

Raymond James prefers to recruit financial advisors one-by-one rather than through acquisitions, because transition assistance fully goes to advisor retention and it lets the firm ensure cultural fit.

Morgan Stanley's advisor-led flows come from both existing advisors and recruits, and the firm is selective while receiving a lot of inbound inquiry from financial advisors wanting to join its platform.
Merrill attracts talent across both new and experienced advisers and has returned to veteran (experienced) broker recruiting after having largely pulled back from it at the end of 2017.

Raymond James targets both new advisors through its Wealth Management Associate and Advisor Mastery programs and experienced advisors (with minimum experience and production qualifications), and also recruits advisor teams and breakaway teams.

Morgan Stanley grants employee loans under a program established primarily to recruit certain Wealth Management financial advisors; the loans are full recourse and due in full upon termination of employment.

Raymond James's Private Client Group recruiting and retention-related compensation includes cash and equity awards issued in conjunction with recruiting activities or as retention for existing advisors, expensed over a requisite service period of typically 5 to 10 years.

Morgan Stanley sponsors deferred cash-based and stock-based compensation programs for financial advisors in the Wealth Management segment that generally contain vesting, clawback and cancellation provisions, which function to retain advisors.
Merrill offers advisors base salary and unlimited earning potential, high-quality leads and direct client interactions, and coaching and mentorship.

Raymond James uses equity (RSU) awards, non-qualified deferred compensation plans and loans to financial advisors as retention tools, and seeks to mitigate retention risk through financial advisor succession planning.
Morgan Stanley pitches the integrated firm as offering unique access to intellectual capital, world-class technology, and compensation that is viewed to be fair and motivating.

Merrill pitches access to its wealth management platform combined with Bank of America's banking and trust capabilities, plus lead generation supported through the global bank, trust division and market presence.

Raymond James pitches a best-of-both-worlds value proposition combining an advisor- and client-focused culture with the resources, platform, technology, products and services advisors can offer clients.

Morgan Stanley's financial supplement reported Wealth Management representatives (financial advisors) of 15,468 as of December 31, 2019, 15,469 as of September 30, 2020, and 15,950 as of December 31, 2020.
Trade press in September 2026 described Morgan Stanley as having close to 15,000 high-producing financial advisors.
As of September 30, 2025, Raymond James reported 8,943 total financial advisors (3,878 employees and 5,065 independent contractors), which it called a record 2% higher than the prior year.
Raymond James reported 8,731 Private Client Group advisors as of March 31, 2025.
According to a trade press report, Merrill executives in October stated that recruited assets to the wealth unit doubled year-over-year as the firm has returned to veteran broker recruiting.
Morgan Stanley's CEO stated in the 3Q26 earnings call that the firm's adviser retention rate is above 99%.
Morgan Stanley reported voluntary attrition of 9% globally in 2025, a figure covering all employees rather than financial advisors specifically.
Merrill's CFO stated in the 2Q26 earnings call that adviser attrition is now at near historic lows, in the context of growing the Merrill sales force.
Raymond James states it has historically had approximately a 1% rate of regretted attrition among financial advisors, and does not see anything large on the leaving side currently.
In the quarter ended December 31, 2024, the departure of primarily one large branch in the Independent Contractor Division reduced assets under administration by approximately $5 billion.

On the 1Q25 call, Morgan Stanley said strong net new assets were supported by positive recruiting trends and that advisor recruitment remains strong, reflecting its reputation as an exceptional place where financial advisors can grow their businesses.

Merrill executives in October 2026 touted that recruited assets to the wealth unit doubled year-over-year, and trade press reports the firm added advisors from rivals representing a combined $1.8 billion in client assets.

For fiscal 2026, Raymond James reported trailing 12-month production of $538 million for recruited advisors coming into its domestic independent contractor and employee channels, up from $407 million the prior year.

The three firms' recruiting and retention approaches can be compared qualitatively but not on a common metric, because each discloses in its own terms: Morgan Stanley in advisor-led recruiting and a >99% adviser retention rate, Merrill in a training program plus experienced hiring and near-historic-low attrition, and Raymond James in culture-led one-by-one recruiting and a roughly 1% regretted-attrition rate.
